_note: Second reading of AI reader 112's anchors, part 2: GHB, sleep across drugs, psychedelics (Liakoni 2018, van Amsterdam 2022, Angarita 2016, Evens 2023, Müller 2022).

tasks.locator: Opioids › Objective measurements, 4th paragraph; Opioids › Subjective measurements, 3rd paragraph; Table 2
tasks.extracted: As summarized: at about the end of the first week of abstinence from heroin, total sleep time, slow-wave, REM and stage 2 sleep were reduced and sleep latency, wake after sleep onset and REM latency increased compared with healthy sleepers (Howe et al.); during the first three weeks, prolonged sleep latency, reduced efficiency and total sleep, more arousals and less slow-wave sleep (Asaad et al.); after six weeks to six months of abstinence from methadone, slow-wave and REM sleep rebounded above baseline.

tasks.locator: Opioids › Opioids and sleep disordered breathing, 1st paragraph; Methadone, 1st paragraph; Buprenorphine, 2nd paragraph
tasks.extracted: As summarized: more than three-quarters of people in methadone maintenance report sleep complaints and about 50% use illicit drugs or medicines to help sleep; between 30 and 90% of patients on long-term opioid therapy show signs of central apnoea in a dose-dependent way; buprenorphine treatment in 70 patients was associated with mild to severe sleep-disordered breathing with hypoxaemia.

tasks.locator: Methods, 1st paragraph
tasks.extracted: The authors describe the paper as a narrative, non-systematic review of human clinical studies; no selection criteria, numbers or appraisal are given.

tasks.locator: Alcohol › Subjective measurements, 1st paragraph
tasks.extracted: As summarized: alcohol loses its sleep-promoting effect with chronic use; clinical insomnia in about 35 to 70% of people with alcohol use disorder depending on setting and stage, against about 15 to 30% in the general population; insomnia is the most frequent complaint after stopping drinking and one of the most refractory problems.

tasks.locator: Alcohol › Objective measurements: Sleep latency, Total sleep time, Slow-wave sleep, Rapid eye movement and Objective sleep quality subsections
tasks.extracted: As summarized: alcohol shortens sleep latency in healthy people; in alcohol use disorder sleep latency is prolonged during drinking and acute and post-acute withdrawal, total sleep time is reduced, slow-wave sleep deficits may take months to years to recover, REM rebounds after stopping with inconsistent findings, and sleep-stage switches are increased from the second night of abstinence to as long as one to two years.

tasks.locator: Alcohol › Relationship between subjective measurements and clinical outcomes, 1st paragraph; Relationship between objective measurements and clinical outcomes, 1st to 3rd paragraphs
tasks.extracted: As summarized: self-reported insomnia during early abstinence predicted drinking or relapse in several studies; longer sleep latency early in abstinence increased the odds of relapse in one study and not in another; slow-wave and REM measures gave mixed results.

tasks.locator: Methods, 1st paragraph; Table 2, Alcohol columns
tasks.extracted: Narrative, non-systematic review; Table 2 marks every early-abstinence alcohol cell as insufficient or conflicting data, while the text describes prolonged sleep latency and reduced total sleep in acute withdrawal.

tasks.locator: Cannabis › Subjective measurements, 1st to 3rd paragraphs
tasks.extracted: As summarized: cannabis may improve subjective sleep in short-term use; with chronic use, withdrawal brings sleep difficulty, strange dreams, insomnia and poor sleep quality, in 32% to 76% of people experiencing withdrawal, in inpatient and outpatient studies and placebo-controlled discontinuation studies; strange dreams typically begin within days of stopping and can persist for weeks; returning to cannabis, alcohol or other sedatives to sleep is commonly observed; the sleep-promoting effect lessens with chronic use.

tasks.locator: Cannabis › Objective measurements, 3rd to 5th paragraphs; Table 2
tasks.extracted: As summarized: tolerance develops to the sleep-inducing and slow-wave effects with chronic use; polysomnography in withdrawal shows increased sleep onset latency and waking, reduced total sleep time, efficiency and slow-wave sleep, and REM rebound, starting from the first night and more noticeable in heavy use, progressing over the first weeks and persisting into abstinence.

tasks.locator: Cannabis › Clinical and laboratory correlates of subjective and objective sleep outcomes, 2nd paragraph; Pharmacotherapy options targeting sleep abnormalities, 1st paragraph
tasks.extracted: As summarized: higher relapse rates were correlated with sleep problems and other withdrawal symptoms, and poor sleep during abstinence contributes to relapse; withdrawal sleep disturbances improve with oral THC or resumption of cannabis use, but the beneficial effects of THC on sleep diminish with chronic use and chronic use leads to more severe sleep problems.

tasks.locator: Methods, 1st paragraph
tasks.extracted: Narrative, non-systematic review; no selection criteria, numbers or appraisal.

tasks.locator: Alcohol › Pharmacotherapy options targeting sleep abnormalities, 1st to 5th paragraphs
tasks.extracted: As summarized: gabapentin studied with largely but not entirely positive results; ramelteon and agomelatine only in case series; quetiapine improved wake after sleep onset and subjective insomnia in a double-blind placebo-controlled trial, with mixed effects on abstinence and re-hospitalization; trazodone benefited sleep measures but in a large placebo-controlled trial was associated with less abstinence during treatment and increased drinking after it; benzodiazepines are often avoided because of addictive potential and overdose risk with alcohol.

tasks.locator: Cannabis › Pharmacotherapy options targeting sleep abnormalities, 2nd to 4th paragraphs
tasks.extracted: As summarized: lofexidine plus oral THC gave the greatest benefit in one study, oral THC alone none; nabilone may reverse withdrawal-related sleep disruption; valproic acid, lithium, nefazodone and bupropion showed no definite benefit; zolpidem, mirtazapine, gabapentin and quetiapine improved sleep parameters but none conclusively reduced relapse.

tasks.locator: Cocaine › Pharmacotherapy options targeting sleep abnormalities, 1st to 3rd paragraphs
tasks.extracted: As summarized: few studies of sleep medicines in people who use cocaine; lisuride changed REM without other benefit; tiagabine increased slow-wave sleep with unnatural architecture and no consistent cognitive benefit; modafinil normalized slow-wave sleep in people who used cocaine chronically, in one study by the senior author's group, with mixed effects on clinical outcome in other trials.

tasks.locator: Opioids › Methadone, 1st paragraph; Buprenorphine, 3rd paragraph
tasks.extracted: As summarized: methadone and electrostimulation were not effective for insomnia in opioid withdrawal; trazodone did not improve subjective or objective sleep in methadone-maintained patients; amitriptyline and lorazepam did not differ on most sleep measures in a randomized double-blind study of 27 people with opioid-withdrawal insomnia.

tasks.locator: Results › Driving Questionnaire and Simulator results, 3rd paragraph; Table 2, No. of collisions and No. of off road accidents rows
tasks.extracted: At the first drive after GHB, every one of the 16 participants had more collisions than after placebo: median 6.5 (range 2 to 19) against 1 (0 to 4), Z = -3.526, p < 0.001, r = -0.62; off-road accidents increased in 7 participants and in none after placebo (Z = -2.375, p = 0.018, r = -0.42); pedestrian hits did not differ.

tasks.locator: Results › Driving Questionnaire and Simulator results, 3rd paragraph; Table 2, Mean speed, Mean speed deviation and Mean lane position deviation rows
tasks.extracted: At the first drive after GHB, speed deviation 4.09 against 2.76 (Z = -3.051, p = 0.002, r = -0.54; greater in 13 of 16) and lane-position deviation 1.93 against 1.23 (Z = -2.896, p = 0.004, r = -0.51; greater in 13 of 16); mean speed did not differ.

tasks.locator: Results › Driving Questionnaire and Simulator results, 1st paragraph; Figure 1 legend
tasks.extracted: All participants rated themselves less able to drive at the first drive after GHB than after placebo (median 4 against 1 on a 1 to 5 scale, p < 0.001); at the second drive the difference remained (p = 0.001), with nearly a third of ratings at 3 or higher; at the third drive it no longer differed.

tasks.locator: Results › Driving Questionnaire and Simulator results, 3rd and 4th paragraphs; Table 2
tasks.extracted: At the second and third drives after GHB no simulator outcome was worse than after placebo; at the third drive speed deviation was greater after placebo (p = 0.017). Within the GHB arm, collisions, off-road accidents and both deviation measures at the first drive were worse than at baseline and at both later drives.

tasks.locator: Methods › GHB and Placebo Dosing, 1st paragraph; Discussion, 7th paragraph
tasks.extracted: Four men developed nausea and vomiting after GHB and could not complete the first post-dose drive; they were replaced and only the 16 completers were analysed. The authors list one dose only, no regular GHB use (possible tolerance), simulator practice effects and no correction for multiple comparisons as limitations.

tasks.locator: Results › 3.3 Residual Cognitive Impairment Following GHB-Use and GHB-Induced Comas, 1st and 2nd paragraphs
tasks.extracted: One Dutch research programme recruited 81 participants in three equal groups (heavy GHB use with multiple GHB-induced comas; regular GHB use without comas; mild polydrug use, never GHB); the coma group performed worst on verbal memory, reported more anxiety, stress, depression and impulsivity, and showed differences in brain activity during memory and emotion tasks.

tasks.locator: Results › 3.3, 3rd paragraph; Discussion, 3rd paragraph
tasks.extracted: No follow-up study of residual impairment after stopping GHB had been done, so reversibility is unknown; the authors state the brain abnormalities may have been present before GHB use and may be a risk factor for it.

tasks.locator: Results › 3.2 Acute Effect of GHB on Cognition in Human Studies, 2nd paragraph; Table 2
tasks.extracted: In 14 laboratory studies (8 to 49 participants each), GHB impaired digit-symbol, memory and psychomotor performance at moderate and higher doses, with modest or no effects at the lowest doses tested; memory impairment was less than with triazolam, pentobarbital or alcohol at the doses compared. None of the listed studies measured thinking on the following days.

tasks.locator: References 55 and 106 to 110; author list
tasks.extracted: All six cited reports on the lasting-effects sample list F. Raposo Pereira and W. van den Brink as authors; both are authors of this review.

tasks.locator: Results › Study selection and sample characteristics, 1st paragraph; Results › Risk of bias, 1st paragraph
tasks.extracted: 48 studies (52 publications), 1774 participants: 16 psilocybin, 16 ayahuasca, 10 LSD, 2 5-MeO-DMT, 3 several, 1 mescaline; sample sizes 6 to 315 (median 18). 14 studies (29%) had a standardized treatment, placebo control and double-blind allocation; 19 (40%) standardized treatment without control or blinding; 15 (31%) were observational.

tasks.locator: Discussion, 2nd and 5th paragraphs
tasks.extracted: Changes were observed most consistently (in 70 to 90% of studies investigating the domain, more than 450 participants each) for depression, stress and grief; mindfulness, acceptance and emotion regulation; personality, values and attitudes; wellbeing; and social effects. At group level no worsening of psychopathology, and no increase in suicidality, manic or psychotic symptoms or decrease in cognitive performance, though few studies assessed these.

tasks.locator: Results › Adverse effects, 1st paragraph
tasks.extracted: 25 studies (52%, 550 participants) mentioned whether they assessed adverse events; 11 (297 participants) reported none; 14 (253 participants) reported 52 headaches (usually lasting no longer than a day or two), 6 insomnia or sleep disturbances, 6 tension, 3 exhaustion, 3 visual distortion, 2 each of fatigue, migraine, nausea, difficulty concentrating and vivid dreams, and single cases including severe anxiety exacerbation with methamphetamine relapse and a psychiatric disturbance lasting one week.

tasks.locator: Discussion › Limitations, 1st and 2nd paragraphs; Methods › Risk of bias, 1st paragraph
tasks.extracted: 72% of studies lacked a control group, double-blind allocation or standardized treatment; only statistically significant effects were summarized; settings with preparation and aftercare mean the results cannot be generalized to recreational use, and selective reporting or publication bias may contribute; the authors present the results as effects observed under favourable conditions, not the average expected effect.

tasks.locator: Results › Flashback phenomena at end-of-study visit, 1st paragraph; Table 2
tasks.extracted: 13 of 142 participants (9.2%) reported flashback phenomena at the end-of-study visit: 7 after LSD only (7.8%), 2 after psilocybin only (8.3%), 4 after both (14.3%). 11 were visual, 2 purely emotional; most lasted seconds (69.2%) or minutes (23.1%), one hours; 53.8% occurred once; in all but two cases they were limited to the week after the last drug administration; over half occurred while relaxing or around sleep.

tasks.locator: Results › Flashback phenomena at end-of-study visit, 2nd paragraph
tasks.extracted: Flashbacks were unpleasant for 2 (1.4% of all 142) and neutral or positive for 10; one case was not documented. No one reported impairment of daily life. One distressing case followed an exceptionally difficult session and the participant left the study; the other was a single episode during escitalopram pretreatment after psilocybin, followed by panic attacks, after which the participant left the study.

tasks.locator: Results › Flashback phenomena at end-of-study visit, 1st paragraph; Flashback phenomena at follow-up, 1st and 2nd paragraphs
tasks.extracted: One participant had about 30 brief, benign visual flashbacks over seven months, which had stopped about ten months before follow-up; at follow-up (mean 31.2 months later, 12 of 13 responding) she was the only one with recurrence after the end-of-study visit.

tasks.locator: Results › Hallucinogen-persisting perception disorder, 1st paragraph
tasks.extracted: No participant met DSM-5 criteria for HPPD; the simulated chance of seeing no case in 142 people was 24.0% at a true incidence of 1%, 5.7% at 2% and 1.3% at 3%. Editors' calculation: zero events in 142 gives a one-sided 95% upper limit of about 2.1%.

tasks.locator: Methods › Inclusion and exclusion criteria of studies, 1st paragraph; Discussion, 1st and 5th paragraphs
tasks.extracted: Exclusions included personal or first-degree family history of psychotic or major psychiatric disorder and more than ten prior illicit drug uses (cannabis excepted). Three of the 13 had also received escitalopram, d-amphetamine or MDMA. The authors list the sample size, varied doses and substances, likely positive attitudes, follow-up only of those with flashbacks, and exclusion of people with mental disorders as limitations.
